rugby.note: Uncountable: play rugby, a rugby match (not "a rugby").

ex: We bought a mini fridge for our small kitchen.
The café sells mini pizzas for kids.
I always carry a mini umbrella in my bag.
Can I get the mini size, please?
mini.note: Often joined to the noun: miniskirt, minibar, minivan.

ex: Winning the cup was a great triumph for our team.
The school concert was a real triumph this year.
The players came home in triumph after the final.
Passing the exam was a small triumph for me.

oops.note: Say it after a small mistake: "Oops, sorry!"

ex: Have you heard her new single on the radio?
The band will release a new single next month.
Their first single was a big hit.
You can download the single for one dollar.
single.note: Most often "single" means one or not married: "a single room", "Are you single?"

voyage.note: A long trip by sea or into space; for other trips say "trip".

ex: She left him after years of abuse.
Emotional abuse can be hard to see from outside.
If you see abuse at home, call this number.
Many people stay silent about abuse in relationships.
abuse.note: Also wrong use: "drug abuse", "abuse of power". It is a verb too: to abuse.

ex: The phone has a bright, clear display.
The display on my watch is broken.
Can you make the display a bit brighter?
This laptop has a bigger display than mine.
display.note: Often a verb, "to show": "The museum displays old cars." "On display" = shown to people.

ex: Is there a supermarket near here?
I buy groceries at the supermarket on Fridays.
The supermarket is open until ten tonight.
She works at the supermarket near our house.
We are having pasta for dinner tonight.
I usually cook pasta with tomato sauce.
How long do I boil the pasta?
Can I have the pasta with chicken, please?
pasta.note: Uncountable: some pasta, a lot of pasta (not "a pasta").

ex: She was a pioneer in computer science.
He is a pioneer of electric cars.
The first pioneers built a small town here.
Our company was a pioneer in online shopping.
He is a total computer nerd.
I was a big nerd in high school.
Are you a movie nerd like me?
My brother is a science nerd and loves space.
nerd.note: Informal; can be friendly or rude.

ex: She showed great enthusiasm for the new project.
The kids greeted us with a lot of enthusiasm.
I love your enthusiasm, but please slow down.
He lost his enthusiasm for the job after a year.
enthusiasm.note: Uncountable: a lot of enthusiasm (not "an enthusiasm").

ex: He is a true patriot and loves his country.
Many patriots joined the army to defend the country.
She calls herself a proud patriot.
You can be a patriot and still criticize the government.

sofa.note: "Couch" is more common in everyday American English.

chili.note: British spelling: "chilli". In the US, "chili" is also a spicy meat dish.

ex: She sent her manuscript to three publishers last week.
The old manuscript is kept in the city museum.
He finished the first draft of his manuscript.
The editor returned the manuscript with many notes.
Don't buy that bag, it's a fake.
Is this painting real or a fake?
The news story turned out to be a fake.
He sold cheap fakes as real watches.
fake.note: Most often an adjective: "fake news", "a fake bag". Also a verb: to fake a smile.

Viking.note: Written with a capital letter: a Viking, the Vikings.

ex: Ask the system administrator for a new password.
She works as an administrator at a hospital.
The administrator manages the company website.
Please contact the administrator if you have problems.
administrator.note: Often shortened to "admin" in everyday speech.

ex: The company changed its logo last year.
The logo is printed on every shirt.
She designed a logo for her friend's café.
Can you make the logo a little bigger?
A tank moved slowly across the field.
The soldiers sat on top of the tank.
Many tanks drove through the city in the parade.
The army sent more tanks to the border.
tank.note: Also a container: "a gas tank", "a fish tank". A "think tank" is a group of experts.

salon.note: Mostly a place for hair, nails or beauty: "a hair salon", "a nail salon".

ex: Bandits robbed the travelers on the mountain road.
The old movie is about a famous bandit.
Police caught the bandit near the border.
The bandits hid their money in a cave.
bandit.note: Sounds old-fashioned; "robber" is more common today.

ex: Public sentiment turned against the new plan.
Market sentiment improved after the good news.
There is strong anti-war sentiment in the country.
I understand the sentiment, but I don't agree.
A cool breeze came in from the sea.
The curtains moved gently in the breeze.
Let's sit outside and enjoy the evening breeze.
There is a nice breeze by the lake today.
breeze.note: Any light wind. Informal: "The test was a breeze" means it was very easy.

ex: He posted a tweet about the game last night.
Her tweet got hundreds of replies in an hour.
Did you see his tweet about the new phone?
I deleted my old tweet because it was rude.
tweet.note: Also a verb: to tweet. The short high sound of a bird is also a tweet.

ex: "Boo!" he shouted from behind the door.
She jumped when her brother said "boo" behind her.
The kids hide and shout "boo" on Halloween.
Don't say "boo" to the baby, she will cry.
boo.note: Also shouted at a bad show: "The crowd started to boo." Slang: "my boo" means my love.

ex: He works in stock trading at a big bank.
Online trading is very popular among young people.
Trading on the stock market starts at nine.
She lost a lot of money in trading last year.
trading.note: Also buying and selling in general: "trading between countries".

ex: The wounded soldier is in a military hospital.
She works as a nurse at the army hospital.
The military hospital is near the base.
Doctors at the field hospital work day and night.
hospital.note: Any hospital, not only for soldiers. US: "in the hospital"; UK: "in hospital".

top.note: Most often "top" means the highest part: "the top of the hill", "on top of the box".

balance.note: Also means staying steady: "I lost my balance and fell." Also "work-life balance".

ex: The Tories won the election in Britain.
My uncle has been a Tory all his life.
Many Tories voted against the new law.
A famous Tory spoke on the radio this morning.
Tory.note: British politics: a member of the Conservative Party. Plural: Tories.

fitness.note: Uncountable: "My fitness is better now" (not "a fitness").

ex: The movie is about a mutant with special powers.
In the comic, the mutants hide from people.
Scientists study mutants of this small fly.
Every mutant in the game has a different power.
She is a food blogger who reviews new cafés.
The food blogger posted a photo of her lunch.
Many restaurants invite food bloggers to try new dishes.
My sister wants to become a food blogger.

trainer.note: For a sports team, "coach" is more common in American English.
